Some properties described as 'inherently difficult to make Decent' due to design or listed status suggest some costs may not be recoverable.
findings.figures: 4,814 homes total, 4,505 surveyed (93.58%), 113 non-decent (2.35%), 45 key component failures, 25 kitchen/bathroom, 43 thermal comfort
findings.quote: Looking ahead over the next 5 years the capital programme will prioritise Decent Homes works with the aim of achieving 100% decent homes compliance at each relevant year-end.

findings.headline: Council explicitly targeted by 'no win, no fee' solicitors encouraging disrepair claims, with 13 new claims in Q1 2025-26
findings.detail: The council is managing 90 disrepair cases total (46 with agreed schedules and works in progress, 26 complete and settled, 18 in litigation). The document explicitly states the council is being targeted by claims management companies. In Q1 2025-26 alone, 13 new claims were raised. Every claim, including those not becoming formal cases, 'has required litigation to defend', creating legal costs regardless of merit.
findings.matters: Deliberate targeting by claims companies creates sustained and unpredictable litigation costs. The trend of 13 new claims in one quarter indicates an ongoing financial exposure rather than isolated disputes. Each defended claim carries legal fees even if settled.
findings.figures: 90 disrepair cases total, 13 new claims in Quarter 1 2025-26, 46 with agreed schedules, 26 complete and settled, 18 in litigation
findings.quote: The Council has been targeted by 'no win, no fee' solicitors who encourage tenants to make disrepair claims against us. Not every live claim has ended up as a formal disrepair case, however each one has required litigation to defend.

findings.headline: 93 properties have outstanding electrical compliance issues requiring prioritization and specialist housing officer input
findings.detail: As of 30 June 2025, of 4,869 properties requiring electrical testing, 98.09% (4,776) have current valid certificates. The remaining 93 properties (1.91%) are split between 66 with out-of-date certificates (1.36%) and 27 needing rewires (0.55%). These constitute capital maintenance liabilities requiring specialist intervention to resolve.
findings.matters: Electrical compliance is a regulatory and safety requirement. The scale of outstanding rewires represents a material capital liability that must be prioritized, and the note that these 'will require specialist housing officer input' suggests remediation will be complex and costly.
findings.figures: 4,869 properties, 98.09% compliant (4,776), 93 outstanding (1.91%), 66 out-of-date (1.36%), 27 requiring rewires (0.55%)
findings.quote: To ensure the outstanding 93 cases (1.91%) are prioritised within the wider housing team as this will require specialist housing officer input.

findings.headline: If the winning bid falls below the independent red book valuation, the council must obtain statutory consents to dispose at a lower price.
findings.detail: The council will instruct independent valuers to update their red book valuation once the Contract heads of terms are agreed. If the capital receipt offered by the winning bidder is lower than this valuation, the council has a legal duty to obtain statutory consents before proceeding, creating a potential obstacle to completion.
findings.matters: There is a material risk that the market receipt for the site may fall short of the council's internal valuation, potentially either reducing the capital receipt or creating a compliance hurdle that delays or prevents the sale.
findings.figures: Capital receipt weighted at 15% of the evaluation scoring; valuation figure not disclosed in this document
findings.quote: If the sale price is lower than the independent red book valuation of the site, then the sale will be conditional on the Council obtaining the necessary Statutory consents to dispose the site

findings.headline: Contract completion is contingent on three separate conditions with an undefined long-stop date still to be confirmed.
findings.detail: The contract completion timeline depends on vacant possession, Secretary of State consents, and constitutional approvals all being satisfied. A long-stop date (marked TBC) will be included to allow rescission if these conditions are not met by a specified date. The timescale is therefore open-ended and currently unconfirmed.
findings.matters: The council cannot reliably forecast when it will receive this capital receipt, which may affect its cash flow planning and ability to rely on this income in financial forecasts.
findings.figures: Completion expected within 12 months of winning bidder notification; planning application within 18 months of completion; development completion within 3 years of planning permission
findings.quote: A long stop-date (TBC) to be included such that the Contract may be rescinded by either party if the events in a. – c. above have not occurred by the long-stop date.

findings.headline: Vacant possession of the Telford Court site has not yet been achieved and completion of the capital receipt depends on it.
findings.detail: The council is actively negotiating with remaining private tenants and leaseholders to achieve vacant possession. This is a mandatory prerequisite for contract completion; the contract will only complete on the last of three conditions, one being that 'the Council achieving vacant possession of the site'. Occupancy levels are described as available only 'upon request', indicating the position remains unresolved.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the timing and receipt of the capital receipt is not indefinitely delayed by occupancy disputes, which may require severance or legal costs to resolve.
findings.figures: Current occupancy levels (number of units privately owned and/or tenanted) not disclosed in this document
findings.quote: the Council is using its best endeavours through negotiations with the last remaining tenants and leaseholders to achieve vacant possession of the site as soon as possible

findings.headline: Property 1 has been vacant and secured since April 2025 due to anti-social behaviour and safety concerns making it unsuitable for continued use
findings.detail: Property 1 (8 bedsits in temporary accommodation) became unsafe due to high levels of anti-social behaviour and rough sleepers accessing it, making it unsafe for council staff to conduct welfare visits. It has been fully vacant since 11 April 2025. Even significant capital investment would not make it suitable due to its layout and design.
findings.matters: An idle asset for six months, combined with service delivery challenges in homelessness and complex needs provision, indicates resource deployment and homelessness management risks that affect financial stability.
findings.figures: 8 bedsits; 1 self-contained studio flat; vacant since 11 April 2025
findings.quote: Due to the nature of the accommodation, Property 1 was primarily used by single males with complex needs. This contributed to high levels of anti-social behaviour and rough sleepers accessing the property. Consequently, it became unsafe for Council officers to carry out their daily health and safety checks and welfare visits.

findings.headline: Homelessness service under significant pressure with 227 households in temporary accommodation, 88 in hotel provision
findings.detail: The council currently accommodates 227 households in temporary accommodation with 88 in hotels—the most expensive form of temporary provision. This demand pressure has driven the decision to convert nine general needs properties to temporary accommodation to replace capacity lost from Property 1's closure.
findings.matters: High hotel temporary accommodation costs consume reserves and put sustained pressure on revenue budgets; this indicates unmet housing demand and financial strain that lenders assess as a risk to budget sustainability.
findings.figures: 227 households in temporary accommodation; 88 in hotels; nine 1-bedroom properties to be converted to temporary accommodation in 2025/26
findings.quote: The homelessness service is under pressure and there are currently 227 households in temporary accommodation of which 88 are in hotels.

findings.headline: Capital receipts from property disposals will reduce the Housing Investment Programme's borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The council plans to sell two properties and reinvest the proceeds into the Housing Investment Programme. The paper explicitly states the funds will be used to reduce the amount the council needs to borrow to fund new social housing development.
findings.matters: Lenders assess debt sustainability; reducing the borrowing requirement demonstrates prudent capital management and improves the council's credit profile.
findings.figures: Two properties being disposed of; capital receipt amounts not disclosed (valuation appendices redacted)
findings.quote: The capital receipts from the disposals will be reinvested into housing, which is more traditional Council housing stock, which will assist in funding new social rented developments and will be used to reduce the borrowing requirement of the Housing Investment Programme.

findings.headline: The council is replenishing general reserves to minimum level while running deficits
findings.detail: The budget includes £500-900k for 'Replenish General Reserves (to increase the minimum level of reserves)' in each of the first three years. This is happening despite the £2m deficit in 2025-26, suggesting reserves were depleted below minimum and the council is prioritising reserve rebuilding alongside deficit management.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion would typically precede a deterioration in creditworthiness. A lender needs to know whether the council can simultaneously rebuild reserves and close material budget gaps.
findings.quote: Replenish General Reserves (to increase the minimum level of reserves) 500 300 200

findings.headline: Interest on borrowings increases 45% over four years, from £1.4m to £2.0m
findings.detail: Interest costs rise from £1,386k in 2025-26 to £2,010k by 2028-29, an increase of £624k. This is accompanied by a growing Minimum Revenue Provision (debt repayment) budget of £3,266k, reflecting a significant capital borrowing programme. The rising interest burden constrains the council's ability to absorb the homelessness cost pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale of the capital programme being funded by borrowing and whether the council can service this debt while managing operational deficits.
findings.quote: Interest on borrowings 1,386 1,800 2,000 2,010 2,010

findings.headline: The council faces £2m budget deficit in 2025-26 and £1.37m in 2026-27 even after approved savings
findings.detail: After all council-approved savings, the 5-year plan shows a £2,000k deficit in 2025-26 and £1,370k in 2026-27. The plan does not specify what further savings, income growth, or reserves will close these gaps. The council only returns to small surpluses from 2028-29 onwards (£624k and £573k).
findings.matters: Material multi-year deficits indicate the council has not yet identified the savings or solutions to balance its budget. This is a material concern for financial sustainability and creditworthiness.
findings.quote: Budget Gap / Excess after Council Approved Savings 2,000 1,370 -283 -624 -573

findings.headline: Homelessness costs are unbudgeted and driving a £2m deficit in 2025-26
findings.detail: The council has estimated additional homelessness costs of £2,000k in 2025-26 alone, on top of £1,041k of grant-funded homelessness prevention. In 2026-27, the ring-fenced homelessness prevention grant cuts to £571k (a 45% reduction) while additional costs remain at £1,000k, creating a structural funding gap. This homelessness pressure is the key driver of the budget deficits.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has a plan to absorb or fund £2m of homelessness costs, and whether grant reductions will force service cuts or further reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Estimated Additional Homelessness Cost: 2,000 (2025-26), 1,000 (2026-27); Homelessness Prevention Grant: 1,041 (2025-26) falling to 571 (2026-27 onwards)
findings.quote: Estimated Additional Homelessness Cost 2,000 1,000 1,000 500 500; Homelessness Prevention Grant (ring-fenced) 1,041 571 571 571 571

findings.headline: Backlog of social housing repairs under Morgan Sindall contract identified as requiring management intervention
findings.detail: The Committee approved adding a report to the next meeting to discuss the Council's options to address a backlog of social housing repairs under its contract with Morgan Sindall. The need for formal discussion of 'options' indicates this is more than routine maintenance and suggests potential performance or budget issues affecting the council's largest asset class.
findings.matters: Deferred social housing repairs reduce asset condition and create future capital requirements; backlog status may indicate contractor performance issues or budget pressures affecting service delivery and financial planning.
findings.quote: to set out the Council's options within its terms of contract with Morgan Sindall to get back on top of the backlog of social housing repairs

findings.paper_title: Budget Report for Housing and Inclusion CTTEE Sept 2025
findings.headline: First Housing Regulator inspection scheduled October 2025 under strengthened 2023 Act compliance framework
findings.detail: Social Housing Regulation Act 2023 (effective April 2024) introduced new consumer standards, tenant satisfaction measures, strict hazard resolution timelines (Awaab's Law), and professional qualification requirements for managers. St Albans faces first inspection 6-8 October 2025. More frequent inspections may follow if concerns are identified.
findings.matters: New regulatory regime brings heightened compliance obligations and reputational/financial risk if inspections identify breaches. Non-compliance could trigger mandatory remediation spending.
findings.figures: First inspection 6-8 October 2025
findings.quote: St Albans first inspection will be 6-8th October 2025. More frequent inspections may occur if the Regulator has concerns.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report for Housing and Inclusion CTTEE Sept 2025
findings.headline: Telford Court decommissioning will result in loss of rental and garage income from major housing asset
findings.detail: Telford Court decommissioning is expected to complete shortly, resulting in permanent loss of rental income and garage income from this site. This reduces the HRA revenue base and asset-backed income streams.
findings.matters: Loss of income-generating assets reduces HRA revenue capacity at a time when HRA finances are already under pressure from deficits and uncertain rents.
findings.figures: Not quantified in document
findings.quote: Telford Court: decommissioning is expected to complete shortly, with the associated loss of rental and garage income from this site.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report for Housing and Inclusion CTTEE Sept 2025
findings.headline: HRA forecast deficit of £6.2m for 2025/26 with rent increase assumption dependent on October CPI publication
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account outturn for 2025/26 is forecast as a net deficit of £6.2m. Rent increase assumptions for 2026/27 remain unknown pending September CPI publication in October 2025. Government has introduced social rent convergence allowing faster rent increases for rents below formula rent level, subject to ongoing affordability consultation.
findings.matters: HRA deficits must be managed from housing reserves and constrain investment in stock maintenance. Uncertain rental income impacts HRA sustainability and service delivery capacity.
findings.figures: £6.2m HRA forecast deficit 2025/26, HRA general reserve £9.4m at 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Budget Report for Housing and Inclusion CTTEE Sept 2025
findings.headline: Planning Appeals reserve exhausted at year-end, having consumed £0.3m in 2024/25
findings.detail: The Earmarked Reserve for Planning Appeals was fully depleted by 31 March 2025 after £0.3m expenditure in 2024/25. Council has budgeted £0.2m replenishment for 2025/26 and £0.1m for 2026/27, assuming Local Plan adoption in Spring 2026. Future appeals demand remains unpredictable.
findings.matters: Depletion of a dedicated reserve for a known risk (planning appeals) suggests material exposure and potential for supplementary funding demands.
findings.figures: £0.3m spent in 2024/25, earmarked reserve exhausted, £0.2m budgeted 2025/26, £0.1m 2026/27
findings.quote: The Earmarked Reserve for Planning Appeals was exhausted at 31/03/25, the Council having spent £0.3m on appeals in 2024/25.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget gap highly uncertain, ranging from £584k surplus to £2.916m deficit across three scenarios
findings.detail: Three budget scenarios developed due to material uncertainties: pay inflation assumption (1% = £195k impact), general inflation (1% = £305k impact), government grant settlement outcome (£0.67m upside to £0.33m downside pending Fair Funding Review conclusion), and homelessness demand. Base forecast shows £470k gap, but worst-case scenario reaches £2.916m including reserve replenishment.
findings.matters: The scale of savings required for 2026/27 remains undefined pending external decisions (government funding review) and internal demand trends, creating planning uncertainty and potential for further service cuts or reserve draws.
findings.figures: Base gap £470k, scenario range £584k to £2.916m, pay sensitivity £195k per 1%, inflation sensitivity £305k per 1%, government settlement range £0.67m to (£0.33m)

findings.paper_title: Budget Report for Housing and Inclusion CTTEE Sept 2025
findings.headline: Homelessness demand crisis: 218 cases with 81 in hotels, creating £1.7m current overspend and £1-2m future pressure
findings.detail: Significant increase in homeless families in 2025/26, with demand for temporary accommodation exceeding available properties. As of end July, 218 cases presented to the council, 81 placed in hotels. Despite efforts to increase TA supply and consider out-of-district placements, hotel accommodation costs are expected to create ongoing pressure of £1.0-2.0m into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory duty with volatile costs that directly erodes current reserves and makes next year's budget dependent on demand trends outside the council's control.
findings.figures: 218 homelessness cases end July 2025 (81 in hotels), £2.0m cost increase in 2025/26, £1.0-2.0m projected pressure 2026/27
findings.quote: There has been a significant increase in the number of Homeless families in 2025/26. Demand for temporary accommodation (TA) has exceeded the number of available properties, resulting in the use of hotels (the number of homelessness cases as at the end of July was 218 of which 81 were in hotels).

findings.paper_title: Budget Report for Housing and Inclusion CTTEE Sept 2025
findings.headline: General Fund reserves forecast to fall £0.9m below minimum level unless 2025/26 overspend is mitigated
findings.detail: The 2025/26 forecast outturn is £1.7m worse than budget, primarily driven by £2.0m increased homelessness costs. If unmitigated, General Fund reserves will fall to £1.6m against the minimum required level of £2.5m, creating a £0.9m shortfall. This significantly impairs the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or emergencies.
findings.matters: Dangerously low reserves are a critical vulnerability for any local authority and directly impact creditworthiness and financial resilience.
findings.figures: £1.7m overspend forecast, £2.0m from homelessness alone, reserves falling to £1.6m vs £2.5m minimum, £0.9m shortfall
findings.quote: Unless mitigations are made to reduce the overspend in 2025/26, the shortfall in reserves against the minimum level is £0.9m, which poses significant financial risks for the council. It reduces the authority's ability to respond to unexpected costs or emergencies, such as economic shocks, service demand spikes, or unforeseen infrastructure failures.

The decision will then be reported back to Full Council after implementation has begun.
findings.matters: Delegated urgent decision-making on capital programme changes signals the council views the homelessness crisis as acute enough to justify expedited governance and compressed timelines. This is a notable governance exception.

findings.paper_title: Drakes Drive Project Update - Amendment to the Capital Programme
findings.headline: 227 households in temporary accommodation with 88 in hotels as of August 2025
findings.detail: The homelessness service faces increased pressure and demand since the Drakes Drive project was identified for development. The council reports 227 households in temporary accommodation, of which 88 are in hotel placements. This demand is explicit justification for the capital reallocation.
findings.matters: High temporary accommodation populations, especially reliance on hotels, typically indicate acute housing stress in the local area and create cost exposure. Hotels are acknowledged as more expensive than property ownership, making this a cash flow and sustainability concern.

findings.paper_title: Drakes Drive Project Update - Amendment to the Capital Programme
findings.headline: £2.86m diverted from housing development to temporary accommodation property purchases
findings.detail: The council is reallocating most of the Drakes Drive/Frobisher Road garage site redevelopment budget (which would have delivered 12-13 three-bedroom houses by 2027/28) to open market property purchases for temporary accommodation. The capital purchases budget rises from £2.28m to £5.14m, while the garage site project budget falls from £3.04m to £0.18m. The original development is judged too slow to meet current demand.
findings.matters: This shows a fundamental reallocation of housing investment from permanent development to temporary accommodation crisis response, driven by operational demand rather than strategy. It reflects acute pressure on the council's homelessness services that has forced deprioritization of long-term development.

Any properties purchased on the open market will be used as temporary accommodation to address the unprecedented demand in services.

news_drafts.headline: Project management controls are applied inconsistently across the council, particularly for smaller projects, creating governance weakness in planning and risk management.
news_drafts.lead: Inconsistent project management can lead to capital schemes running over budget or time, affecting financial forecasting. This is a governance control weakness relevant to capital delivery and value for money.

news_drafts.headline: Procurement team experienced capacity constraints during 2025/26 that led to delays in procurement activities, though no statutory breaches occurred.
news_drafts.lead: Procurement delays affect capital project delivery and contract management efficiency. Capacity constraints in this control function indicate a governance weakness that could affect the council's ability to execute projects efficiently.

news_drafts.headline: Homelessness is identified as a significant financial pressure in 2025/26 with SLT actively considering strategies to manage costs.
news_drafts.lead: Homelessness costs are a growing pressure across local government that councils cannot easily control. Identifying it as significant suggests costs may exceed budget or require reserves to be deployed.
